longForm.title: The Battle of Ap Bac, 1963: The Warning That Was Not Heeded
longForm.excerpt: On 2 January 1963, a Viet Cong battalion held its position against a South Vietnamese force four times its size, shot down five helicopters, and inflicted 80 ARVN casualties before withdrawing at night. The battle demonstrated everything that was wrong with the war effort two years before the first American ground troops arrived.
paragraphs: The Battle of Ap Bac on 2 January 1963 occurred at a moment when the American public had been told, by the Kennedy administration and by Military Assistance Advisory Group commanders in Saigon, that the counterinsurgency effort in South Vietnam was succeeding. The strategic hamlet program was being presented as effective. ARVN forces were being trained and equipped to a standard that, by American assessments, should have made them capable of handling the Viet Cong Main Force units they faced. The battle that unfolded in a rice field outside the village of Ap Bac in Dinh Tuong Province on the first working day of 1963 demonstrated, with the clarity that comes from documented failure, that the assessment was wrong. The demonstration was available to anyone who read the after-action reports. The institutional response was to dispute the reports.

The tactical situation at Ap Bac was not complicated. American signals intelligence had located the 514th Viet Cong Local Force Battalion — approximately 320 men — in the village. The ARVN 7th Division was tasked with encircling and destroying it. The plan used three converging ground elements, helicopter-borne infantry, and armored personnel carriers from the ARVN 2nd Armored Cavalry Squadron. The force available to the ARVN numbered approximately 1,400 men against 320 Viet Cong. The terrain was flat rice paddy with tree lines providing cover for the defenders. On paper, the outcome should not have been in doubt.

The battle went wrong from the opening helicopter assaults. ARVN infantry, inserted by UH-1B helicopters into an exposed landing zone near the Viet Cong position, immediately took heavy fire and refused to advance against the tree line. American advisors — including Lieutenant Colonel John Paul Vann, who was the senior US advisor to the ARVN 7th Division and whose role in the battle became the central fact of the subsequent dispute — ordered ARVN commanders to advance and were refused. The M113 armored personnel carriers of the 2nd Armored Cavalry approached the tree line and were met with intense fire from Viet Cong using recoilless rifles and automatic weapons; the tracks halted at the water's edge of the rice paddy rather than pressing the assault. Three UH-1 helicopters were shot down in the opening phase. Two more were subsequently damaged and forced down. Five helicopters lost or damaged in one engagement — the Viet Cong had been trained specifically in helicopter countermeasures.

John Paul Vann's after-action report, which circulated to MACV and eventually to the Pentagon, was a document of unusual candor. Vann attributed the failure to ARVN unwillingness to close with the enemy, to the paralysis of armored forces that should have been decisive, and to command failures at multiple levels of the ARVN chain of command. The report identified the ARVN 7th Division's commanding general, Brigadier General Huynh Van Cao, as having given orders that prevented a successful engagement. The report was accurate. The institutional response from MACV, under General Paul Harkins, was to characterize Ap Bac as a victory: the Viet Cong had been driven from their position, the report argued, and had suffered significant casualties. Vann, who had counted the Viet Cong dead himself and found far fewer than MACV claimed, was furious. Harkins's characterization prevailed in official communications to Washington.

The press reporting from Ap Bac told a different story. Neil Sheehan, then a UPI correspondent, and David Halberstam of the New York Times were both present or arrived quickly afterward and reported the battle as the failure it was. The resulting conflict between the official military narrative and the press accounts was the opening round of a dispute that would characterize American journalism's relationship with the Vietnam War throughout the 1960s. Harkins complained to Washington about the correspondents. Ambassador Frederick Nolting suggested that the negative reporting was harming the war effort. The Kennedy administration's public affairs approach sought to manage the story rather than address the facts it reflected. The facts — that ARVN forces under American-approved commanders had failed to engage a significantly inferior force and had lost five helicopters doing it — were not changed by the management effort.

The significance of Ap Bac in the longer history of the Vietnam War rests on what it should have revealed about the war's fundamental assumptions. The Diem government's ARVN, whatever its equipment and training levels, was not consistently willing to close with the enemy in the aggressive manner that the counterinsurgency strategy required. The reasons for this were structural: ARVN commanders whose careers depended on the political favor of Ngo Dinh Diem had strong incentives to avoid casualties and preserve their forces, because a defeated commander could be dismissed while a cautious one survived. American advisors could recommend, they could argue, they could write damning after-action reports. They could not command. The command authority remained with ARVN officers who were operating under a different set of institutional incentives than the strategy required.

Vann left Vietnam in frustration in 1963, convinced that the war effort was failing and that the official assessments were disconnected from reality. He returned to Vietnam as a civilian AID official in 1965 and spent the rest of the war there, becoming one of the most influential — and most controversial — American figures of the conflict. Neil Sheehan's eventual biography of Vann, A Bright Shining Lie, published in 1988, used Vann's experience at Ap Bac and afterward as the central thread of its account of how the United States prosecuted and lost the war. The title came from the bureaucratic fictions that American military and civilian officials sustained in the face of contrary evidence — the kind of fiction that Harkins had offered about Ap Bac in January 1963.

The lessons of Ap Bac that were available in January 1963 — that ARVN would not always fight, that official statistics were not reliable, that the command relationship between American advisors and South Vietnamese units was insufficient to produce the results the strategy required — were lessons that the American escalation of 1965 proceeded without adequately incorporating. The escalation answered the problem of ARVN's willingness to fight by substituting American ground forces for South Vietnamese ones, which solved the tactical problem at Ap Bac at the cost of creating the strategic problem that Ap Bac had first illuminated: a war whose political sustainability depended on South Vietnamese ownership, fought by a force that the United States was substituting itself for.

shortForm.title: The Helicopter at Ap Bac: Innovation Under Fire
shortForm.excerpt: At Ap Bac in January 1963, the Viet Cong shot down five American helicopters using techniques they had specifically trained for. The loss forced an immediate reassessment of airmobile tactics. It was the first major demonstration that the helicopter — the defining weapon of the Vietnam War — was not invulnerable.
paragraphs: The UH-1 Iroquois helicopter had been in service with US Army aviation units advising the ARVN since 1962, and by January 1963 it was the cornerstone of the airmobile concept that the Army was developing in parallel with its Vietnam advisory mission. The helicopter offered mobility that ground-bound forces could not match: the ability to insert troops rapidly at any accessible point, to resupply isolated positions, to evacuate wounded, and to maintain reconnaissance coverage of jungle terrain that was opaque to ground observation. The Army's faith in the helicopter was substantial enough that it had authorized the 11th Air Assault Division specifically to test airmobile doctrine. What the helicopter had not yet been seriously tested against was an enemy that had been trained to engage it.

The Viet Cong's antiaircraft training in 1962 and 1963 was rudimentary by any technical standard — the weapons were small arms and light machine guns — but the techniques were sound. Ground fire against low-flying helicopters was most effective when the shooters held fire until the aircraft was committed to a landing approach, when it was slowest and lowest. At Ap Bac, the 514th Battalion waited. The first helicopters carrying ARVN troops came into the landing zone at low speed and low altitude. The concentrated ground fire from the tree line destroyed the first two aircraft before they completed their descent. Subsequent aircraft, warned by radio, altered their approach angles but remained vulnerable; three more were shot down or damaged beyond repair during the battle.

The operational response to Ap Bac's helicopter losses was rapid and substantive. Approach and departure angles were revised. Suppression doctrine was updated: landing zones required pre-assault fire before the first aircraft committed to the approach. The subsequent development of the armed helicopter — the UH-1 Huey gunship and eventually the AH-1 Cobra — was accelerated in part by the recognition that the troop-carrying helicopter needed escort by armed aircraft capable of suppressing ground fire during approaches. The tactical adaptations were well-designed. They did not eliminate helicopter vulnerability; the war would cost the United States approximately 5,000 helicopters of all types, a casualty figure that reflected eight years of continuous operations under fire. But they reflected the ability of the aviation community to learn from Ap Bac in ways that the strategic community did not.

onThisDay.headline: Union VI Corps Attacks Confederate Positions at Salem Church During the Battle of Chancellorsville
onThisDay.summary: On 4 May 1863, Major General John Sedgwick's Union VI Corps, having captured Marye's Heights the previous day, advanced west along the Orange Plank Road toward Chancellorsville and engaged Confederate forces under Jubal Early and Lafayette McLaws at Salem Church. The engagement stalled Sedgwick's attempt to relieve Hooker's beleaguered Army of the Potomac. Hooker withdrew across the Rappahannock the following night, ending the Chancellorsville campaign.
